prompt: Why does the lesson say importance cannot order Coreto's queue of four items?
hint: How did each item get into the room?

choices.text: Importance is too hard to estimate
choices.why: The difficulty is not estimation; even a perfect measure of importance would rank four things that all matter.

choices.text: Each item matters to somebody already
choices.why: Right: the order depends on what waiting costs and how long each takes, not on importance.

choices.text: The CTO decides importance, not the team
choices.why: Who decides is not the lesson's point; deciding by seniority is one of the habits it rejects.

choices.text: Only customers can say what is important
choices.why: Deciding by the loudest customer is another habit the lesson rejects: visible complaints are not the size of a cost.

prompt: The four items cost R$ 108,000 a week while they wait, and take 25 weeks of the group's time in all. Run in parallel, all four finish in week 25. What is the delay cost, in reais?
hint: The whole weekly cost runs for every week.

prompt: Which two facts about an item does the lesson say decide its place in the queue?
hint: One belongs to product, one to engineering.

choices.text: Its sponsor's seniority and its visibility
choices.why: Those decide most meetings, and the lesson's point is that they should not.

choices.text: Its value to customers and its risk
choices.why: Both feed the cost of delay, and a queue needs the duration beside it.

choices.text: Its cost of delay and its duration
choices.why: Right: what each week of waiting costs, and how many weeks of the group it takes.

choices.text: Its number of complaints and its age in the backlog
choices.why: Complaints show a cost exists without measuring it, and age in the backlog measures nothing.

prompt: Process-management lesson 12 already orders a queue with WSJF in relative points. What does doing it in reais add?
hint: Points produce a ranking. What else can money do?

choices.text: A different order from the one points give
choices.why: The calculation is the same; with consistent estimates the order agrees. What changes is what you can do with the result.

choices.text: Precision: money estimates are exact
choices.why: The lesson calls them estimates and is honest about it; precision is not the gain.

choices.text: An order's total, comparable with the budget
choices.why: Right: two orders can be compared in reais, and the gap compared with an engineer-year or a budget line.

choices.text: Speed: a money estimate takes less time to agree
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says it is quicker; it asks for written assumptions, which takes longer.

prompt: Match each habit of estimating cost of delay to what the lesson says it buys.

pairs.right: Every item can stand in one queue
A wrong estimate shows which part was wrong

pairs.left: Product owns value, engineering owns duration

right_distractors: The most senior sponsor settles disputes

prompt: Festival organisers sign their season's contracts on a known date. How does the lesson say festival seat maps should be handled then?
hint: Nothing is lost until the date.

choices.text: Ranked by CD3 like the others
choices.why: A fixed-date item put through a steady-rate formula comes out in the wrong place.

choices.text: Done first, since a deadline is the most urgent thing
choices.why: Nothing is lost before the date, so doing it first spends weeks other items needed.

choices.text: Dropped, because its cost of delay is zero for now
choices.why: Zero now and everything after the date is the fixed-date shape; dropping it loses everything.

choices.text: Scheduled to land before the date
choices.why: Right: ask about the shape before running the arithmetic.

prompt: Coreto's Data team estimates the cost of delay of its own debt work, alone, and brings the number to planning. What does the lesson predict?
hint: Who owns which half of the estimate?

choices.text: Product discounts the number the moment it sees it
choices.why: Right: product owns the value side; an estimate nobody from product shaped is one product does not believe.

choices.text: The number is accepted, as engineers know the debt best
choices.why: Engineers know the duration best; the value of waiting is product's half.

choices.text: The debt work wins, since it carries interest
choices.why: Interest is part of a cost of delay; it wins only if the estimate is believed and the CD3 is higher.

choices.text: The estimate is fine as long as it is in reais
choices.why: One unit is one habit of three; who estimated is another.

prompt: Reinertsen's advice: if you quantify one thing about your work, quantify its cost of ___.
Pix in instalments costs R$ 48,000 a week of delay and takes 12 weeks. What is its CD3, in reais per week of work?
hint: Cost of delay divided by duration.

prompt: Put Coreto's four items in CD3 order, highest first.
hint: Divide each cost of delay by its weeks: 30,000/6, 48,000/12, 18,000/3, 12,000/4.
trap: Putting Pix first orders by cost of delay alone and ignores that it takes 12 weeks while the others wait.

prompt: Shortest first: seat-hold fix (3 weeks, R$ 18,000 a week), partner API (4, R$ 12,000), festival seat maps (6, R$ 30,000), Pix in instalments (12, R$ 48,000). What is this order's delay cost, in reais?
hint: Each cost of delay times the week the item finishes: 3, 7, 13, 25.

prompt: Why does putting Pix ahead of the seat-hold fix cost Coreto more than the reverse?
hint: Who waits, and for how long?

choices.text: Pix has the smaller cost of delay
choices.why: Pix has the largest cost of delay, R$ 48,000 a week; the order turns on duration as well.

choices.text: The fix would wait 12 weeks; Pix waits only 3
choices.why: Right: 12 × R$ 18,000 = R$ 216,000 against 3 × R$ 48,000 = R$ 144,000. The pairwise swap is the CD3 comparison, R$ 6,000 against R$ 4,000.

choices.text: The policy in lesson 1 says so
choices.why: The policy agrees, and the arithmetic stands without it; that agreement is the point.

choices.text: Pix needs the seat-hold fix to be finished before it starts
choices.why: No dependency is described between them; the order comes from cost and duration.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the group's hours, priced at R$ 150, the wrong number for choosing an order?
hint: Does the payroll change between orders?

choices.text: R$ 150 an hour is out of date
choices.why: The rate is fine; any rate would cost the same in every order.

choices.text: Hours ignore the cloud bill
choices.why: The cloud bill has nothing to do with the order of these four items.

choices.text: They cost the same in every order, so they do not separate the choices
choices.why: Right: what differs is what those hours would have produced elsewhere, the opportunity cost.

choices.text: Engineers underestimate how long things take
choices.why: That is a real problem with durations, and not the reason given here.

prompt: With all four items still waiting, a director inserts a two-week change ahead of the queue. What delay cost does the queue pay for it, in reais, before counting what the change is worth?
hint: The whole queue waits two more weeks at R$ 108,000 a week.

prompt: What does Davi put in front of Júlia when she argues for Pix first? Choose all that apply.
hint: What the order costs, what it buys, and what would change it.

choices.text: What Pix first costs in delay overall
choices.why: Yes: R$ 162,000, the opportunity cost of that order.

choices.text: That his item is more important than hers
choices.why: That is the argument the sheet exists to replace.

choices.text: A question about whether her estimate for Pix is too low
choices.why: Yes: a higher estimate is what would change the answer, so the inputs are open.

choices.text: A ruling that the order is settled
choices.why: The lesson calls the argument an invitation to check the inputs, not a verdict.

prompt: Two items in another company's queue have the same cost of delay a week, and one takes twice as long as the other. By CD3, which goes first?

choices.text: The longer one, since it needs the head start
choices.why: Starting the long one first makes the short one wait the whole time, at the same weekly cost.

choices.text: The shorter one
choices.why: Right: its CD3 is twice the other's, and the long one loses less while it waits.

choices.text: Either: equal cost of delay means a tie
choices.why: Equal cost of delay with different durations is exactly the case CD3 separates.

choices.text: Both together, splitting the team
choices.why: Splitting makes both finish at the end, the most expensive arrangement.

prompt: Pix takes 12 weeks. Above what cost of delay a week would Pix overtake the seat-hold fix, whose CD3 is R$ 6,000?
hint: Pix's CD3 has to pass R$ 6,000.

choices.text: R$ 54,000 a week
choices.why: That is R$ 18,000 × 3, the fix's own numbers; Pix's threshold uses its own 12 weeks.

choices.text: R$ 72,000 a week
choices.why: Right: R$ 6,000 × 12 weeks. Above that, Pix's CD3 passes the fix's and Pix leads.

choices.text: R$ 48,000 a week
choices.why: That is Pix's current estimate, which gives a CD3 of R$ 4,000.

choices.text: R$ 96,000 a week
choices.why: That would put Pix well ahead, at R$ 8,000; the threshold is lower.

prompt: CD3 is cost of delay divided by ___.
At Coreto the CD3 order agrees with lesson 1's guiding policy. What does the lesson say to do when a sheet and a policy disagree?

choices.text: Follow the policy: strategy outranks arithmetic
choices.why: The policy may be the wrong one; the disagreement is a reason to look, not to pick a side.

choices.text: Follow the sheet: numbers beat opinions
choices.why: The sheet is built from estimates, and an estimate can be the wrong part.

choices.text: Find out which one is wrong
choices.why: Right: either an estimate or the policy itself is wrong, and finding which is a better use of the meeting than either side insisting.

choices.text: Split the difference between the two orders
choices.why: A compromise order hides which input was wrong and pays for both mistakes.
